analysis.one_liner: Requires aircraft makers to provide safety equipment to airlines at no extra charge.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote in the House and died in committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require manufacturers of large passenger planes to provide safety-enhancing equipment — things like terrain and weather advisories, angle of attack indicators, sensor 'disagree' alerts, and backup fire suppression systems — to airlines at no additional charge, rather than selling them as optional extras. It also directs the Federal Aviation Administration to set performance standards for that equipment and require it to be installed on all large passenger aircraft. It was introduced in December 2019 and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers, who would get safety equipment installed on the planes they fly on without it being an optional add-on the airline has to buy separately. Airlines would receive the equipment at no charge and gain a public list of what safety features manufacturers offer.

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers of large passenger aircraft to offer or provide non-required safety-enhancing equipment to airlines without an additional charge, within two years of enactment.
Creates an FAA program to identify, classify, and approve such safety equipment, with published evaluation criteria covering situational awareness, independent warnings, and occupant protection.

Directs the FAA to set performance standards for angle of attack indicators, sensor disagree alerts, and backup fire suppression systems, and to require certified versions to be installed and operated on all large passenger aircraft within 30 months after certification procedures begin.

Requires manufacturers to report annually to the FAA every safety feature they offer, with the lists published on a public website so regulators and the public can see what safety equipment exists and which airlines are getting it.

analysis.who_pays: Aircraft manufacturers, chiefly the large planemakers that build Part 121 aircraft, would have to provide safety equipment without charging for it and would face new certification requirements and annual reporting obligations as a condition of holding their production certificates.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not explain how manufacturers would absorb the cost of providing safety equipment for free, and its one-year deadline for the FAA to establish performance standards for three categories of equipment is faster than the agency's typical rulemaking pace, raising questions about whether the mandate could be implemented as written.

The equipment would no longer be 'optional,' so the bill effectively converts items that airlines previously chose to buy into mandatory installations across the fleet, a shift some would argue should happen through the FAA's regular certification process rather than a statutory deadline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefits are real and targeted: the equipment named in the bill — angle of attack indicators, sensor disagree alerts, and backup fire suppression — addresses known causes of commercial aviation accidents. The main cost is that planemakers would bear the expense of providing and certifying the equipment, and the compressed timelines could produce rushed standards. On balance, the bill trades a modest, identifiable cost on a small number of manufacturers for safety features on every large passenger plane.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Aviation Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on December 11, 2019.
The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the day it was introduced, and the next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation.
The bill attracted no cosponsors during its time in the House.
No further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Aircraft manufacturers benefit from the outcome: they avoided a requirement to provide safety equipment to airlines without charge and the new certification and reporting obligations. Passengers get none of the equipment the bill would have mandated.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up; it was referred to the Aviation Subcommittee and received no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors signed on from either party, so the bill's failure drew no visible partisan support or opposition; it simply never moved.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from charging airlines for safety equipment that is not federally required, converting add-on safety features into free standard equipment, and would impose new certification and annual reporting duties. A manufacturer whose business model includes selling safety equipment as priced options loses that revenue under the bill.

Airlines would receive certified safety equipment at no charge and gain a public record of what safety features exist, but would also be required to install and operate the newly mandated equipment across their fleets.

Passengers are the intended beneficiary: the bill would put angle of attack indicators, sensor disagree alerts, and backup fire suppression systems on every large passenger aircraft, with performance standards set by the FAA.
